title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Pulp & Paper Mills
description: MPI and mag particle testing on US pulp and paper mill digesters, boilers, liquor tanks and dryer cans. Technicians travel to your mill. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Pulp and Paper Mills in the US
html:
Magnetic particle inspection for pulp and paper mills in the United States is the surface examination most mills reach for when they suspect cracking on carbon steel in alkaline service. Atlantis mobilizes SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to your mill to examine digester welds, boiler attachment welds, liquor tank nozzles, dryer can welds and repair areas, and returns a report with sketches of every indication. To scope a mill outage, request an MPI inspection quote.

Why mills use mag particle testing on kraft equipment

Most of the pressure equipment in a kraft mill is carbon steel, and carbon steel is ferromagnetic, so a magnetic field passes through it and is disturbed by a crack that reaches the surface. Fine particles gathered at the disturbance make the crack visible to the technician within seconds of applying them. That is the whole case for the method: it is direct, it is sensitive to tight cracks, and it works through a thin layer of paint or light surface oxide when the technique is demonstrated for the coating in place.

The weakness is equally plain. The method shows only surface and near-surface flaws, it needs a ferromagnetic part, and it says nothing about wall loss. Thickness questions belong on the UT page for pulp and paper, and cracks in stainless or other nonmagnetic material belong on the PT page.

Digester welds and caustic cracking

API 571 describes caustic stress corrosion cracking as a mechanism in carbon steel exposed to hot caustic solutions, and kraft pulping liquors are exactly that kind of environment. Cracks start at welds and cold-formed areas where residual stress is high and, historically, where post-weld heat treatment was omitted. In a digester, that points the examination at longitudinal and circumferential seams, nozzle-to-shell welds, support attachments and any weld repair made after commissioning.

Wet fluorescent magnetic particles under ultraviolet light are the usual choice, because the contrast of a fine crack against a darkened, scale-free weld is hard to match with visible-light powder. Inside a vessel, that means controlling ambient light, using a UV lamp with a stated intensity at the work surface, and keeping the surface free of liquor residue that fluoresces or masks the indication. The technician records the black-light intensity and the ambient light level on the report.

Where a crack is found, our report gives location, orientation and length against the weld map. We do not size depth or decide repair scope. Your engineer takes our findings, and the sizing and repair decision follow from there. If a thickness check around the cracked area is also wanted, the ultrasonic work can be scoped in the same mobilization.

Boiler attachments, headers and dryer can welds

Power and recovery boilers are examined under state boiler law, which adopts ASME Section I for construction and the National Board Inspection Code, NBIC, for repairs and alterations. Surface examination is commonly called for on welded attachments, header and drum nozzle welds, and the weld buildup left after a repair. For repairs, the magnetic particle examination of the finished weld is often the record your jurisdictional inspector asks to see before the equipment returns to service.

Dryer cans and Yankee dryers present a different surface. Cast iron and steel dryer shells are ferromagnetic, but they are often machined, polished or ground, and a rough casting surface raises the background that the technician must read through. We use a procedure that matches the finish: smooth shells call for light, controlled particle application, and rougher castings may call for a different particle contrast. Rotating equipment must be locked out and secured before anyone applies a field, and the mill's lockout procedure governs that.

Tanks, nozzles and structural attachments

Black, white and green liquor tanks have shell-to-bottom welds, nozzle reinforcement pads, roof support attachments and manway frames, and each is a stress concentration. On the exterior, we examine the bottom-to-shell corner weld and attachment welds that can be reached from grade or scaffold. Our tank inspection page covers the wider scope for storage vessels, including how the tank program ties to API 653 where a mill uses it.

Lifting lugs and rigging points are a recurring MT job in mills. Where a mill lifts heavy equipment during an outage, ASME B30.20 or its own rigging program may call for examination of welded lifting attachments before use. We examine the welds and report indications by location; the rigger or engineer decides whether the attachment can be used.

Technique details for mill conditions

  • Surface preparation. Liquor scale and deposits must be removed to clean metal. Wire brushing, grinding or blasting is done by the mill or its cleaning contractor, and the scope states the finish expected at each weld.
  • Magnetization. An AC electromagnetic yoke is the standard field-source for weld examination on site. ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709 set the lifting-force check and the requirement to examine in two directions across each area.
  • Particle type. Wet fluorescent particles for fine cracking in clean weld zones, dry powder where a hot or rough surface makes liquid carriers impractical.
  • Temperature. Carrier liquids and particle suspensions have temperature limits, and surfaces that exceed them are examined after cooling or with a technique shown to work for that temperature.
  • Verification. The yoke lift test and a pie gauge or equivalent field-indicator check are recorded at the start of work, as the procedure requires.
  • Demagnetization and cleaning. Residual fields are checked when the part will be welded or machined next, and particle residue is removed so coating and insulation can follow.

Repair welds, grinding and re-examination

A large share of mill MT work follows maintenance rather than preceding it. When a crack is ground out of a digester seam or a boiler header, the excavation is examined before welding to confirm the crack is gone, and the finished weld is examined again after grinding to blend. Each step is a separate indication-free record, and the sequence matters to the inspector of record, so the report keeps the steps in order with the weld repair number the mill assigns.

Post-weld heat treatment, where the repair procedure calls for it, is another point on that timeline. Examination after heat treatment confirms that no cracking developed during the thermal cycle. Because the exact point in the sequence is set by the repair procedure and not by the examiner, we ask for the procedure at quotation so the scope lists each examination point in order.

Codes, regulators and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 7 is the examination method, and the code of construction, usually ASME Section I for boilers or Section VIII for pressure vessels, supplies the acceptance criteria. NBIC governs repairs, state boiler law decides who inspects, and mill programs sometimes add BLRBAC recommendations for recovery boilers. TAPPI technical information papers on digester and tank inspection often sit in the mill's reference library, though they are guidance and not law. Atlantis reports each indication against the criteria you name. Accept and reject calls belong to the owner and the inspector of record, and we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service.

What the MT report contains

Each report lists the component or weld identification, the procedure and revision, the equipment used with serial numbers, the yoke lift-test result, the particle and carrier type, surface condition, and the technician's name and SNT-TC-1A level. Every indication appears on a sketch with location, orientation and length, with a photograph where the procedure calls for one. Acceptance or rejection is recorded against the named criteria, and an ASNT Level III reviews the report before issue.

What to send for a quote

  • Weld map or list of components with tag numbers
  • Material and thickness, and whether it is clad or stainless anywhere
  • Governing code and the acceptance criteria to use
  • Surface condition and who prepares it, including scale removal
  • Expected surface temperature and any insulation or coating
  • Vessel entry details, confined space permit process and access method
  • Site address, badge or orientation requirements, outage dates once known

Outage planning for US mills

Magnetic particle work follows cleaning and precedes coating, so it lands in the middle of the outage when scaffolds are up and entry permits are active. Entry into digesters and liquor tanks falls under 29 CFR 1910.146 and your permit program. Fluorescent work is slower in vessels where light cannot be controlled, so the scope notes which areas will need curtains or lighting changes. The mill supplies power for equipment and lighting, and our technicians travel to your site with the yokes, lamps and particle supplies needed. See also the turnarounds and shutdowns page.

Training mill technicians in MT

If your reliability team wants its own people examining welds between outages, MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training follow SNT-TC-1A, and the magnetic particle simulator offers practice before live parts. Your company writes its own procedures and certifies its personnel under its written practice. We can help produce the procedure your inspector will review, and the background reading is in the magnetic particle testing guide and the Article 7 explainer. The national method page is magnetic particle testing.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and we do not offer specialist techniques for cracking in the stainless layer of composite recovery boiler tubes. Welds also often need a visual examination first; for weld-specific scopes see weld inspection.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on stainless steel in a pulp mill?
faq.a: Only on ferromagnetic grades. Austenitic stainless steel is not magnetic, so bleach plant piping and cladding are examined by liquid penetrant instead. Duplex and martensitic grades vary, and we confirm magnetic response on the actual part.

faq.q: Will MPI find caustic cracks in digester welds?
faq.a: Yes, when the cracks open to the surface and the weld is cleaned to bare metal. Wet fluorescent particles under UV light are the usual choice. Cracks below the surface or behind scale can be missed, so the scope states the surface preparation required.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to mag particle work?
faq.a: The limits come from the procedure and the particle carrier, and they are stated on the report. Hot surfaces are examined after cooling or with a technique demonstrated for that temperature, and a location that was too hot is recorded as not examined.

faq.q: Can you inspect through coatings or paint?
faq.a: A thin nonmagnetic coating may be acceptable when the procedure demonstrates that the technique still reveals known indications beneath it. Heavier coating is removed at the test location, and the maximum coating thickness is set on the procedure.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The code of construction supplies criteria, and your inspector of record accepts or rejects the equipment. We report each indication with location and length against the criteria you name, and the owner or engineer makes the repair decision.

faq.q: Do you examine dryer can welds while the machine is running?
faq.a: No. Dryer cans must be stopped, locked out and secured before examination, and the mill controls those steps. Technicians then examine welds and shell surfaces that the mill has opened up and cleaned.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MPI on a recovery boiler or digester?
faq.a: A component list with tag numbers, weld maps or drawings, material, the governing code, surface condition, temperature, entry and access details, and the site badging steps. With that we can set method, coverage and technician days.

faq.q: Do you provide the fluorescent lamp and yoke?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site with their own yokes, UV lamps, particle supplies and calibration check tools. The mill provides power, lighting control, access and any lockout needed.

faq.q: When is MT the wrong method for a mill component?
faq.a: It is the wrong method for wall loss, for nonmagnetic material, and for flaws buried under heavy scale or deep in a weld. Use ultrasonic thickness testing for wall loss and penetrant testing for stainless or aluminum surfaces.
